text: Right now, you are flying through space at up to one thousand miles per hour.
You just can't feel it.
So what would happen if the Earth suddenly stopped spinning?
Our planet turns once on its axis roughly every twenty-four hours.
At the equator, that means a speed of about sixteen hundred and seventy kilometers per hour.
You, the air and the oceans all move together, so everything feels perfectly still.
Now imagine the planet stops in an instant.
The ground would halt… but you would not.
Anything not anchored to the bedrock would keep going east, at hundreds of miles per hour.
People, cars and loose rocks would be swept across the land.
The atmosphere would keep moving too.
Near the equator, the winds would be several times faster than the strongest hurricane ever recorded.
They would scour the surface and whip up enormous storms.
The oceans would not stay put either.
Earth's spin makes the planet bulge at the equator, and the seas bulge with it.
Without that spin, according to computer simulations, the water would slowly flow toward the poles.
The result: two giant polar oceans, and one huge continent wrapped around the middle of the planet.
Then there is the light.
A planet that does not spin still travels around the Sun.
So a single day would last a whole year: about six months of daylight, then six months of night.
One side would bake, while the other would freeze in the dark.
There could also be a hidden danger.
Earth's magnetic field comes from liquid iron moving deep in the core.
Some scientists think that without rotation, this field could weaken, leaving us less protected from the solar wind.
The good news: there is no known way for Earth to stop suddenly.
But it is slowing down, very gradually, because of the Moon's tides.
Each century, the day gets longer by roughly two thousandths of a second.
Back when dinosaurs were alive, a day was a little shorter than it is today.
So the next time you stand still, remember: you are riding a giant spinning ball.
